overview.title: Matrix product box diagram, higher-rank products, and the start of reshaping
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations
overview.main_topic: Finishing naive_matrix_product, visualising shape compatibility with the box diagram of figure 2.5, extending the product rule to higher-rank tensors, and introducing tensor reshaping via the MNIST reshape call.
overview.central_idea: In a product x • y = z, the width of x must equal the height of y, and z inherits x's height and y's width; the same trailing-axis/leading-axis rule extends to tensors of any rank. Reshaping is a third essential tensor operation, already used to flatten MNIST images.
overview.importance: The box diagram is the mental tool the authors say you will draw constantly when designing models; the higher-rank rule is what makes matmul work on batched and multi-axis data. Reshaping is how raw data tensors (images) get turned into the matrices Dense layers expect.
learning_objectives: Complete and explain the last two lines of naive_matrix_product.
Read figure 2.5: identify a, b, c, the row of x, the column of y, and where z[i, j] lands.
Apply the higher-rank product rules (a, b, c, d) • (d,) → (a, b, c) and (a, b, c, d) • (d, e) → (a, b, c, e).
Explain what tensor reshaping is for and recognise the MNIST reshape (60000, 28 * 28).
prerequisites: Matrix–matrix product rule x.shape[1] == y.shape[0] and the first part of naive_matrix_product (p.57)
The MNIST preprocessing that flattened images (p.44)

summary:
The page begins with the last two lines of `naive_matrix_product` from p.57: inside the double loop, `z[i, j] = naive_vector_product(row_x, column_y)` and finally `return z`. Every coefficient of the product is thus a vector product between row `i` of `x` and column `j` of `y`.

To make shape compatibility intuitive, the authors present **figure 2.5**, a *box diagram*: `x`, `y` and `z` are drawn as rectangles — literal boxes of coefficients. `x` has shape `(a, b)` (height `a`, width `b`), `y` has shape `(b, c)` (height `b`, width `c`), and `z = x • y` has shape `(a, c)`. Because the rows of `x` and the columns of `y` must have the same size, the *width of x must match the height of y*; in the figure a highlighted row of `x` and column of `y` meet at the small cell `z[i, j]`. The authors remark that if you go on to design new machine learning algorithms you will be drawing such diagrams often.

The product then generalises to higher-dimensional tensors with the same compatibility rule: `(a, b, c, d) • (d,) -> (a, b, c)` and `(a, b, c, d) • (d, e) -> (a, b, c, e)`, "and so on". The last axis of the first operand is matched against the first axis of the second and contracted away; the remaining axes are concatenated.

Subsection **2.3.4 Tensor reshaping** opens: reshaping is a third essential tensor operation. It was not used inside the `Dense` layers of the first example, but it was used in preprocessing: `train_images = train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28))` turned the `(60000, 28, 28)` image tensor into a `(60000, 784)` matrix before it was fed to the model. The definition (same coefficients, rearranged to a target shape) and examples follow on p.59.

paragraphs.what_it_means: A geometric picture replaces the symbolic rule `x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]`: when the boxes are placed so that `x` sits to the left of `z` and `y` sits above `z`, matching sizes become matching edges.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Shape errors are the most common bug in model code; a diagram you can sketch in seconds prevents them.

paragraphs.what_it_says: In the figure `x`, `y` and `z` are rectangles of coefficients. Since rows of `x` and columns of `y` must have equal size, the width of `x` equals the height of `y`. Readers who develop new ML algorithms will draw such diagrams often. The product also generalises to higher-rank tensors with the same compatibility rules as the 2-D case.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Reading figure 2.5: `x.shape = (a, b)`, `y.shape = (b, c)`, `z.shape = (a, c)`. The shared `b` is the horizontal extent of `x` and the vertical extent of `y`; the highlighted row of `x` (length `b`) and column of `y` (length `b`) are the two vectors dotted to produce the single highlighted cell `z[i, j]`. `z` is as tall as `x` and as wide as `y`.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The picture encodes three facts at once — the compatibility condition, the output shape, and how each output entry is computed — which is why the authors recommend drawing it.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in the diagram, sliding the highlighted row down through `x` and the column across `y` sweeps out every cell of `z`; that sweep is exactly the `for i … for j …` double loop.

terminology.meaning: Side lengths in figure 2.5: a = rows of x and z; b = columns of x = rows of y (contracted); c = columns of y and z.

connections: p.57: 'the coefficients are the vector products between the rows of x and the columns of y'.
p.46: matrices as grids of numbers.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Following the two printed higher-rank examples, the authors note that the pattern continues for any ranks.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The two code lines above state the rule: `(a, b, c, d) • (d,) -> (a, b, c)` — contracting a rank-4 tensor with a vector along the last axis removes that axis; `(a, b, c, d) • (d, e) -> (a, b, c, e)` — contracting with a matrix replaces the last axis `d` by the matrix's second axis `e`. In both cases the last axis of the first operand must equal the first axis of the second.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is how a Dense layer can act on a batch of sequences, e.g. `(batch, time, features) • (features, units) -> (batch, time, units)`, without any explicit loop over the batch or time axes.
paragraphs.technical_idea: General pattern (as implied by the examples): `(…, d) • (d, …) -> (…, …)` — the shared axis `d` is summed over and the remaining axes of both operands are concatenated in order.

terminology.meaning: The axis shared by both operands that is summed over and disappears from the result (d in the examples).

connections: p.57: 'a tensor product generalizes to tensors with an arbitrary number of axes'.
p.50: real-world data tensors with 3–5 axes that such products act on.

paragraphs.excerpt: A third type of tensor operation that’s essential to understand is tensor reshaping.
paragraphs.what_it_says: After element-wise operations and tensor products, the third essential operation is tensor reshaping. It did not appear inside the `Dense` layers of the first example but was used in preprocessing the digit data: `train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28))`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The MNIST images arrive as a rank-3 tensor `(60000, 28, 28)`; the `Dense` layer expects a matrix with one row per sample, so each 28 × 28 image is unrolled into a 784-long vector, giving `(60000, 784)`. The total number of values is unchanged (60000 × 784 = 47,040,000).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Reshaping is the glue between data layout and layer expectations: images, sequences and other multi-axis data constantly need to be flattened or unflattened. The next page defines it precisely and introduces transposition as a special case.

terminology.meaning: Rearranging the coefficients of a tensor into a new shape with the same total number of elements (defined on p.59).

connections: p.44: the original preprocessing code in the MNIST example.
p.59: definition of reshaping, examples, and transposition.

concepts.name: Matrix product (box-diagram view)
concepts.definition: For x of shape (a, b) and y of shape (b, c), z = x • y has shape (a, c), and z[i, j] is the vector product of row i of x with column j of y.
concepts.intuition: Draw x to the left of z and y above z; x's width must equal y's height, and z fills the rectangle whose height comes from x and width from y.
concepts.technical: $z_{ij} = \sum_{k<b} x_{ik} y_{kj}$; completed by the two final lines of naive_matrix_product on this page.
concepts.significance: The authors say you will draw this diagram often when designing algorithms; it is the fastest way to check layer shapes.
concepts.example: Figure 2.5: x (a, b), y (b, c), z (a, c).
concepts.misconception: That z has the shape of x or of y. It takes its height from x and its width from y.

concepts.name: Higher-rank tensor product rule
concepts.definition: The product of tensors of any rank follows the 2-D compatibility rule: the last axis of the first operand must equal the first axis of the second; it is contracted and the remaining axes are concatenated.
concepts.intuition: Treat all leading axes of the first operand as 'batch' axes that are carried through unchanged.
concepts.technical: (a, b, c, d) • (d,) → (a, b, c); (a, b, c, d) • (d, e) → (a, b, c, e); and so on.
concepts.significance: Lets a single matmul apply a weight matrix to every item in a batch (or every timestep in a sequence) at once.
concepts.misconception: That the two tensors must have the same rank. Only the one shared axis must match.

concepts.name: Tensor reshaping
concepts.definition: A tensor operation that rearranges a tensor's coefficients into a target shape with the same total number of elements.
concepts.intuition: Unrolling a 28 × 28 grid of pixels into one long line of 784 pixels — same values, different arrangement.
concepts.technical: `train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28))` maps (60000, 28, 28) to (60000, 784). Formal definition and examples on p.59.
concepts.significance: Needed whenever the data layout differs from what a layer expects; the MNIST example used it before the first Dense layer.
concepts.example: The reshape line on this page.
concepts.misconception: That reshaping changes the data. It changes only the arrangement; the count and values of coefficients are preserved.

code.what_it_does: Inside the double loop over rows i of x and columns j of y, stores the vector product of row_x and column_y into z[i, j]; after the loops, returns the completed (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]) matrix.

Return z once all a × c cells are filled.

code.inputs_outputs: Together with p.57: inputs x (a, b), y (b, c); output z (a, c).
code.algorithm: a · c vector products of length b.
pitfalls: The indentation shows line 1 is inside both loops and line 2 is at function level; copy the full function from p.57–58 before running.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: the complete function as printed across p.57-58, plus a check
import numpy as np
def naive_vector_product(x, y):
    z = 0.0
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        z += x[i] * y[i]
    return z

def naive_matrix_product(x, y):
    assert len(x.shape) == 2
    assert len(y.shape) == 2
    assert x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]
    z = np.zeros((x.shape[0], y.shape[1]))
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        for j in range(y.shape[1]):
            row_x = x[i, :]
            column_y = y[:, j]
            z[i, j] = naive_vector_product(row_x, column_y)
    return z

x = np.random.random((2, 3)); y = np.random.random((3, 2))
assert np.allclose(naive_matrix_product(x, y), x @ y)

code.title: Shape rules for higher-rank tensor products
code.what_it_does: Not runnable code — a notation showing how output shapes follow from input shapes when a rank-4 tensor is multiplied by a vector or by a matrix.

line_explanations.explanation: Product with a vector of length d: the shared axis d is contracted, leaving (a, b, c).
Product with a matrix (d, e): d is contracted and replaced by e, leaving (a, b, c, e).

code.inputs_outputs: Left operand's last axis must equal right operand's first axis.
code.algorithm: Same as the 2-D rule applied along the last/first axes; leading axes act as batch axes.
pitfalls: In NumPy, np.matmul with ndim > 2 treats leading axes as a batch and multiplies the last two axes — consistent with these rules for the cases shown.

t = np.random.random((2, 3, 4, 5))
print((t @ np.random.random((5,))).shape)    # (2, 3, 4)
print((t @ np.random.random((5, 6))).shape)  # (2, 3, 4, 6)

line_explanations.explanation: `.reshape` takes the target shape tuple; 28 * 28 evaluates to 784. The number of coefficients (47,040,000) is unchanged.

code.algorithm: Reinterpret the same memory with a new shape (no data is copied for a contiguous array).
code.theory_link: Formula m3; definition of reshaping on p.59.

deeper.title: Reading figure 2.5 step by step
deeper.body:
1. Bottom-left box: `x`, height `a`, width `b`. A horizontal strip is highlighted — a 'Row of x'.
2. Top-right box: `y`, height `b`, width `c`. A vertical strip is highlighted — a 'Column of y'.
3. The two highlighted strips have the same length `b`: that is the compatibility condition (`x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]`).
4. Bottom-right box: `z`, height `a` (aligned with `x`), width `c` (aligned with `y`).
5. Extend the highlighted row to the right and the highlighted column downward; they cross at the small green cell `z[i, j]`, whose value is their dot product.
6. Repeat for every row and every column to fill `z`.

deeper.title: Higher-rank products as batched matrix products
deeper.body: Beyond the book: `(a, b, c, d) • (d, e) -> (a, b, c, e)` can be read as `a·b·c` independent matrix–vector-style operations — or, grouping differently, as a single matrix product after reshaping: flatten the leading axes to get `(a·b·c, d)`, multiply by `(d, e)` to get `(a·b·c, e)`, then reshape back to `(a, b, c, e)`. This equivalence (reshape → 2-D matmul → reshape) is how many frameworks actually implement such products, and it ties the two topics on this page — tensor product and reshaping — together.

deeper.title: Why MNIST needed a reshape and the Dense layers did not
deeper.body: A `Dense` layer computes `matmul(input, W) + b`. With `W` of shape `(784, 512)`, the box-diagram rule says the input must have width 784, i.e. shape `(samples, 784)`. The raw images are `(60000, 28, 28)` — width 28, not 784 — so they are reshaped once before training. Inside the network, each layer's output is already a matrix `(samples, units)` that matches the next layer's `W`, so no further reshaping is needed. (My synthesis of p.44, p.57 and this page.)

deeper.title: Jigsaw edges
deeper.body: Think of `x` and `y` as jigsaw pieces: `x`'s right edge has `b` tabs and `y`'s top edge has `b` slots. They only fit if the counts agree. Once joined, the combined piece `z` spans `x`'s height and `y`'s width. Leading axes in higher-rank products are just stacks of identical puzzles solved in parallel.

questions.question: In figure 2.5, x has shape (a, b) and y has shape (b, c). Which statement is correct?
options: The height of x must equal the height of y
The width of x must equal the height of y, and z has shape (a, c)
The width of x must equal the width of y, and z has shape (b, b)
questions.answer: The width of x must equal the height of y, and z has shape (a, c)
questions.explanation: The text says 'the width of x must match the height of y' (both are b), and the figure labels z.shape as (a, c). Heights (a vs b) and widths (b vs c) need not match, and (c, a) reverses the output axes.

questions.question: Using the rules on this page, what is the shape of (a, b, c, d) • (d, e)? And of (32, 10, 64) • (64,)?
questions.answer: (a, b, c, e); and (32, 10) for the second case.
questions.explanation: The shared axis d (or 64) is contracted; the leading axes remain and the right operand's remaining axis e (if any) is appended. For a vector right operand nothing is appended.

questions.question: Let x = [[1, 0, 2], [0, 1, 1]] (shape (2, 3)) and y = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]] (shape (3, 2)). Compute z = x • y following naive_matrix_product.
questions.explanation: z[0,0] = 1·1 + 0·3 + 2·5 = 11; z[0,1] = 1·2 + 0·4 + 2·6 = 14; z[1,0] = 0·1 + 1·3 + 1·5 = 8; z[1,1] = 0·2 + 1·4 + 1·6 = 10. Each cell is the vector product of a row of x and a column of y; the shape is (a, c) = (2, 2).

questions.question: Why do the authors suggest you will often draw box diagrams like figure 2.5?
questions.answer: Because the diagram makes shape compatibility visible — matching edges show which axes must agree and what the output shape is — which is essential when developing new algorithms whose tensor shapes must line up.
questions.explanation: The text says 'If you go on to develop new machine learning algorithms, you'll likely be drawing such diagrams often'; the picture encodes the compatibility condition, output shape and per-cell computation at once.

questions.answer: A tensor of shape (60000, 784) with the same pixel values rearranged
questions.explanation: Reshaping to (60000, 28 * 28) flattens each 28 × 28 image into a 784-vector; values are unchanged and the sample count stays 60000. Normalisation is a separate step; (784, 60000) would be a transpose; 784 is the number of pixels, not images.

questions.question: Reshaping was not used inside the Dense layers of the first example. Where was it used instead?
questions.answer: In preprocessing: the digit images were reshaped from (60000, 28, 28) to (60000, 784) before being fed into the model.
questions.explanation: The text states it was used 'when we preprocessed the digits data before feeding it into our model', with the reshape line shown.

questions.question: Sketch figure 2.5 from memory for x of shape (3, 4) and y of shape (4, 2): label a, b, c, mark where z[2, 1] comes from, and state z's shape.
questions.answer: a = 3, b = 4, c = 2; z[2, 1] is the dot product of row 2 of x (length 4) with column 1 of y (length 4); z has shape (3, 2).
